summary: A culinary history of confit, a preservation technique that began with slow-cooking duck or goose in its own fat in Gascony and has spread worldwide. The note describes how chefs in Italy, Morocco, Japan, Barbados and San Francisco have adapted it with olive oil, shoyu, sugar syrup and sous-vide. It closes with sustainability concerns about the fats and ingredients used.
one_line: Confit evolved from a Gascony fat-preservation method into a global, adaptable technique shaped by regional chefs and modern sustainability concerns.
key_facts: The word 'confit' comes from the French verb 'confire,' meaning "to preserve."
The note says records of confit date back to the 4th century BCE.
Confit originated in the Gascony region of France, where abundant ducks and geese and the seasonal chill led to the technique.
Medieval cooks salted meat, then slowly cooked it in a low-temperature oven covered in rendered fat, creating an anaerobic environment that inhibited bacterial growth.
On September 5, 2023, chef Etienne Gauthier taught immersive confit workshops in Gascony and said "Confit is not just about duck."
In Gauthier's workshop, duck legs were seasoned with salt, herbs and spices, cured overnight, rinsed, and cooked in melted duck fat at no more than 200°F.
On November 16, 2023, chef Alessandro Rossi introduced olive oil in place of animal fat for confit at a culinary conference in Rome, confiting garlic, tomatoes and lemons.
Moroccan cuisine uses confit lemon as a staple in tagines and pastillas.
On November 23, 2023, chef Hina Yamamoto unveiled confit mackerel with a shoyu base at the Tokyo Gastronomy Symposium.
On December 4, 2023, chef David Weekes of Barbados demonstrated citrus confit, saying the sugar in the syrup works like fat by drawing out moisture; he made confit lime peel.
On February 2, 2024, chef Olivia Taylor used a sous-vide machine to confit root vegetables in butter and thyme at a San Francisco pop-up dining event.

On September 19, 2024, Lars Nielsen spoke at the International Culinary Sustainability Conference in Copenhagen, urging ethical animal fats and plant-based oils and attention to the environmental impact of ingredients.
